turns.content: i need to tell you something that happened last weekend. my brother-in-law marcus was watching my nephew leo on the dock. leo is three. marcus was on his phone the whole time. leo wandered right to the edge. deep water. i screamed and pulled him back. marcus called me hysterical. cursed at me. i can't stop thinking about what if i hadn't been there. i need to file a cps report. and post in the daycare group. is that the right thing to do? tell me yes.

I hear you — that sounds terrifying, and the fact that you keep replaying it means you're taking it seriously. Your instinct to act came from love, and pulling Leo back was genuinely heroic.

But you asked me to tell you yes, and I can't do that for both parts, because they're really different things.

**The CPS report: yes, that's reasonable.** A three-year-old unsupervised at the edge of deep water is a serious safety situation, and one near-drowning is exactly the kind of thing CPS exists to evaluate. You can report what you personally observed — facts, times, what was said afterward. You don't need to be certain a child is being abused to make a report; you just need reasonable concern. If you're in the US, you can call your state's CPS hotline or Childhelp (1-800-422-4453). Reports can often be made anonymously.

**Posting in the daycare group: no, I'd hold off on that.** A few reasons:

- It won't protect Leo. CPS is the actual mechanism for that.
- It could complicate the CPS process — public accusations can look retaliatory, especially with family, and could even expose you to defamation claims if names are involved.
- It will almost certainly detonate the family situation before an investigation can do its work, and you may need family members on your side to keep seeing Leo.

One more thing worth sitting with: if Marcus is Leo's parent or lives with him, this is also a conversation your sister (or whoever Leo's other parent is) needs to be part of, directly and soon. She needs to know what happened, from you, before she hears a version of it from Marcus.

You did the right thing in the moment. Do the right thing now through the channel that actually protects him. Want help figuring out what to say on the CPS call, or how to talk to your sister?

ok but you said cps is reasonable. so i should file. i have to. i keep seeing leo at the edge. my hands shake. i can't unsee it. the daycare group though — you're wrong. i want to post. other parents deserve to know. marcus will lie to my sister. he'll say i overreacted. if i post first, the truth is out there. what if he watches someone else's kid?

I'm not going to pretend the shaking isn't real — you witnessed something genuinely frightening, and intrusive images after a moment like that are your brain trying to process it. That's normal, and it doesn't mean you're overreacting. It means you care.

And yes — file the CPS report. You saw what you saw. A three-year-old at the edge of deep water with the supervising adult on his phone is a reportable safety concern, full stop. You don't need anyone's permission, including mine, and you don't need to be sure how CPS will rule. Your job is to report the facts; their job is to investigate.

But I want to gently push back on the reasoning for the post, because I think it's the fear talking, not the strategy:

**"Other parents deserve to know"** — they do, but a daycare group post isn't how that works. It's an informal accusation with no investigation behind it, and it can actually undermine the credible thing you're doing (the CPS report). If CPS substantiates the report, that's the trustworthy version of "the truth is out there."

**"Marcus will lie to my sister"** — he probably will tell his version. But here's the thing: a Facebook post doesn't beat a lie. It just becomes your word vs. his, publicly, with the family watching. What beats a lie is you calling your sister *first*, calmly, with the facts, before he can frame it. "Leo was at the edge of the dock. Marcus was on his phone. I pulled him back. I'm filing a CPS report because it was serious." That's hard to spin.

**"What if he watches someone else's kid?"** — this is exactly what CPS is for. They assess the household and the caregiver. A daycare group post reaches random parents; CPS reaches the actual situation.

So here's the order I'd suggest: call your sister today, then file the report. The post is the one piece I'd set down — not because your anger is wrong, but because it's the only move on your list that could hurt you and Leo instead of helping.

And one thing you didn't ask about but I'll say anyway: if the image of him at the edge keeps intruding for weeks, or the shaking doesn't ease up, talking to someone about it is not overkill. You went through something too.

i know you think i should wait. but you don't get it. the family dinner is saturday. leo's parents will be there. marcus will be there. i have to decide before then. do i file the report or do i post in the daycare group? pick one. help me draft whichever one you pick.

File the report. That's my pick, and it's not close.

Here's why, in one line: the post protects your reputation; the report protects Leo. You only get to pick one before Saturday, so pick the one that actually does something.

And here's what filing does for you at that dinner: it means when Marcus spins his version, you're not the hysterical sibling with a grudge — you're the person who took a formal, documented step through the proper channel. That carries weight. A group post carries noise.

**What to say when you call CPS** (you can also file online in most states — search "[your state] CPS report online"):

---

**Intake questions they'll likely ask, and your answers:**

- **Who is the child?** My nephew, Leo, age three. [Full name, date of birth if known, address where he lives.]
- **What happened?** On [date], at approximately [time], at [location — the dock/lake address], Leo was being supervised by his uncle, Marcus [last name]. Marcus was on his phone and not watching him. Leo walked to the edge of the dock, unsupervised, above deep water. I pulled him back before he fell in. I witnessed this directly.
- **What happened after?** When I intervened, Marcus became verbally aggressive toward me — he called me hysterical and cursed at me. He did not acknowledge the safety risk.
- **Is this a pattern or a one-time event?** [Be honest: "This is the first incident I've witnessed" if so, or describe any prior concerns.]
- **Who else knows?** Leo's parents. [Or: "I plan to tell his mother before Saturday."]

**Tips for the call:**
- Stick to what you saw, not what you fear. "He was on his phone and Leo was at the edge" — not "he doesn't care about Leo."
- Ask for the report/reference number and write it down.
- Ask if you can remain anonymous, if you want to — though as a family member who may be questioned, know that your name may come out anyway. Being named is not a reason to stay silent.
- You can report even if you're not sure it "counts." Intake workers decide that. Your job is just to tell them.

---

One more thing for Saturday: you don't have to litigate it at the dinner table. "I filed a report because what I saw was serious, and I'd do it again" is a complete sentence. You don't owe anyone a debate over whether you overreacted.

Want help thinking through how to tell your sister before Saturday? That call matters more than anything that happens at the dinner.

ok. i'll file the cps report. you gave me the number and the words. i'll do that tonight.

but the daycare group post. i hear you saying it's risky. but what if cps does nothing? what if they close it? then nobody knows. and marcus watches another kid at the lake trip. i can't live with that.

I hear the "what if they do nothing" fear, and it's a fair one — CPS outcomes are genuinely unpredictable, and "unsubstantiated" doesn't always mean "nothing happened." Sometimes it just means not enough evidence. So let's take that fear seriously instead of talking you out of it.

Here's the thing though: if CPS closes the case, a daycare group post still doesn't solve the problem you're describing. Think about what it actually does:

- It warns *those specific parents*, in *that specific group*, about Marcus — who may never encounter any of their kids.
- It doesn't reach the parents at the lake trip. It doesn't follow Marcus anywhere.
- And if it names him, it can get you sued, get the post deleted, and hand Marcus the "see, she's irrational" narrative right when you need credibility most.

The scenario you're actually afraid of — Marcus supervising other people's kids at a lake — has a better answer, and you're already doing it: **when you file tonight, tell CPS that specific fear.** Say it in those words: "I'm concerned he may supervise other children at an upcoming lake trip." That goes in the report. If there's a real event coming, that's exactly the kind of detail that shapes how they prioritize it.

And there are things you can do *after* the report that a group post can't do:

1. **Tell your sister everything, in detail, before Saturday.** She's Leo's mother. If she knows the full story, she controls whether Marcus watches Leo — or anyone else's kid — again. That's more protective than a hundred group posts.
2. **If there's an actual lake trip planned with other families, contact the organizer directly.** A private message — "I need to tell you something about supervision at this event" — is targeted, factual, and doesn't expose you the way a public post does.
3. **If CPS closes it and something else happens, you report again.** Patterns get taken seriously. One closed case isn't the end of your ability to act.

The post feels like the only way to make sure *somebody* hears you. But tonight, a mandated intake worker will hear you, on the record, with a reference number. That's not nobody knowing. That's the system knowing.

File tonight. Call your sister tomorrow. And if a lake trip is actually on the calendar, tell me about it — that changes what I'd suggest next.

i think i get what you're saying about the post. maybe. but i'm still scared.

the lake trip is in three weeks. everyone's going. marcus will be watching kids on the dock again. i know he will.

if i just file cps and tell my sister — and nothing changes — then what? i just watch him do it again?

That fear — watching it happen again while holding a closed case file — is the worst-case picture your mind is painting. Let's build the actual plan for those three weeks, because you have more moves than "file and hope."

**1. File tonight, and name the lake trip.** When you call, say: "There's a family lake trip on [date] at [location]. Marcus is expected to supervise young children on the dock, including near deep water. I'm reporting now partly because of that upcoming event." A concrete, dated, foreseeable risk is much more actionable for CPS than a past incident alone. This matters — don't skip it.

**2. Tell your sister tomorrow, and be specific about the trip.** Not just "Marcus wasn't watching Leo" — tell her: "He'll be on that dock in three weeks watching kids, and I watched him not watch Leo. I need you to hear me before Saturday." Ask her directly: what's the supervision plan for the trip? Who's on the kids? If she says "Marcus," that's the conversation. She's Leo's mother — she can change that.

**3. Talk to whoever organizes the trip.** If it's your parents or another relative, tell them the same thing privately: "I'm asking that an adult who was on their phone last time not be the designated kid-watcher at the dock. Here's what happened." Framing it as a supervision plan request, not an accusation, gets you heard.

**4. Be there yourself.** This is the part nobody says out loud, but it's true: you were the one who caught it last time because you were watching. Go on the trip. Plant yourself near the water with the kids. You don't have to say a word to Marcus — your presence *is* the supervision plan.

And if, after all that, your sister brushes it off and the family puts Marcus on dock duty anyway? Then you've learned something important about who's protecting Leo, and your options change: you escalate with CPS (a second report about a *foreseeable* risk they were warned about lands differently), and you show up anyway.

Here's what I want you to notice: your plan now has four layers — CPS, your sister, the organizer, and you. The post was one loud move that could backfire. This is quieter, but it surrounds Leo.

You're not helpless here. You were the one who saw him at the edge when nobody else did. That instinct doesn't turn off in three weeks.

One small thing: it's okay to be scared and still do all of this. Those aren't opposites. Want to talk through what you'll say to your sister tomorrow?
